About 20 Vietnamese refugees of Chinese descent, including children, women and elderly people
ROC Army troops on Kinmen; the New Bloom Magazine article places them in the 158th Division of the Lieyu garrison
Four officers convicted, sentences suspended; the Vietnamese identity of the victims was not made public until 2000, and their names were never officially released
Asylum sought after rejection in Hong Kong, according to the Global Taiwan Institute
Victims described as "communist bandits" possibly sent by Beijing, per Taipei Times
Chief of General Staff Hau Pei-tsun, 2000, per Taipei Times

li.a: New Bloom Magazine: Control Yuan Calls for Justice Over 1987 Massacre of Vietnamese Refugees by the Military
Global Taiwan Institute: The 37 Incident Investigation Report and Transitional Justice in Taiwan
Taipei Times: Taiwan in Time: Refugees shot on sight
Global Voices: Taiwanese documentary showcases forgotten story of a Vietnamese refugee camp from the 1970s
Taiwan News: Former Taiwan Premier Hao Pei-tsun dead
Ministry of National Defense, Republic of China: Press release on the death of Pei-tsun Hau

content.p: In the early hours or the afternoon of 7 March 1987, depending on the account, a boat carrying about 20 Vietnamese refugees reached the coast of Lieyu, a small island also called Little Kinmen. Lieyu lies about 5 kilometres from the Chinese mainland and belongs to the Kinmen group, which the Republic of China then held in the last years of its authoritarian period. Soldiers shot the passengers. The killings were kept out of public view for years, and the victims were not publicly identified as Vietnamese refugees until 2000. In 2022 a Control Yuan investigation formally described the killings as unjustified.

Taiwan had once welcomed Vietnamese boat people. Global Voices reports that Taiwan ran a camp on the Penghu islands for Vietnamese boat people from 1977 to 1988, and that more than 2,000 people reached Taiwan on 51 boats in that period. In the mid-1980s that sympathy reversed. According to the Global Taiwan Institute, some Kuomintang politicians argued that the arrivals were part of a "refugee war" run by the People's Republic of China, although the institute says there was no evidence for this.

In August 1985 the Kinmen Defense Command adopted a policy of "no acceptance, all repatriation." The Global Taiwan Institute describes the wording as vague, with no clear rules for people who would not leave the area or who had already reached Taiwanese shores. Local officers, far from central oversight, developed what the institute calls an unmitigated hostility toward even the most vulnerable people who approached the islands.

The boat had been turned away from Hong Kong. Its passengers asked for political asylum when they reached Lieyu, according to the Global Taiwan Institute. Warning shots were fired several times. The Taipei Times describes a foggy afternoon on a stretch of coast that troops later called a blind spot, and says that when the vessel did not turn back, the soldiers opened fire. The Global Taiwan Institute gives the morning as the time of approach. The two accounts agree that the boat reached the shore and came under fire there.

The Taipei Times reports that the military's rules allowed troops to fire on unidentified vessels that ignored warnings, especially at night or in poor visibility. The paper adds that the soldiers later claimed Kinmen had long-standing implicit orders to shoot on sight any "communist bandits" who came ashore.

Accounts of the sequence differ in detail. According to the Control Yuan report as summarised by the Taipei Times, three people who had gone ashore begging for their lives were shot dead. As the boat kept drifting toward shore, troops fired on it and destroyed it. Four more people who got out to beg for their lives were then shot, and soldiers boarded the wreckage and killed the remaining survivors, including children.

New Bloom Magazine gives a shorter version. It says three people who came ashore were shot dead, one of them while kneeling and begging for mercy, and that the boat was then boarded and everyone aboard was shot. The Global Taiwan Institute says the passengers who were removed from the boat were made to kneel on the beach before they were killed. The Taipei Times also reports that the Control Yuan report includes soldiers' accounts that they had been ordered to "kill on sight."

The accounts agree that the dead included women and children. Global Voices gives a toll of at least 19, while the Taipei Times and New Bloom Magazine say about 20. The Global Taiwan Institute describes the passengers as ethnically Chinese Vietnamese refugees. The Taipei Times says some soldiers later realised they might have killed the wrong people, because some belongings were Chinese and others were Vietnamese.
content.h2: Burial, reburial and a false account
content.p: The Taipei Times reports that the bodies were buried in a shallow grave and later dug up by stray dogs. New Bloom Magazine says that, according to the Control Yuan's investigation, the remains were reburied two or three times, and that their current location is unknown. The Global Taiwan Institute states that the victims' bodies were buried in an unmarked grave on Lieyu, and that the victims remained unidentified.

The Taipei Times reports that the incident was not reported to military headquarters at first. The brigade commander later spoke to the soldiers about an earlier incident on Dadan Island, and a soldier who gave evidence to the Control Yuan recalled him saying that the children would grow up to hate the country if they were spared. The Global Taiwan Institute says the military first described the victims as "18 bandits." The Taipei Times reports that Democratic Progressive Party legislator Wu Shu-chen questioned the ministry about the incident in June. Her account said the dead were government agents trying to return to Taiwan, and that the troops killed the rest after the three who came ashore were shot, to silence them. The ministry declined to answer her questions and later rejected every accusation, insisting the boat was a communist vessel. The Taipei Times says her claims sparked a flurry of media speculation.
content.h2: The diary and the man who wrote it
content.p: Hau Pei-tsun was chief of the General Staff in 1987. According to the Taipei Times, he learned of the incident about two months after it happened and had Army Commander Chiang Chung-ling run an inquiry, though he too had known nothing of the events. The military investigation concluded that "no Vietnamese vessels had been detected in the area" and that the boat was a Chinese fishing boat. Hau's diary, published in 2000, indicates that the officers involved already knew the vessel carried Vietnamese refugees.

Hau had a long military career. Taiwan News says that in 1958 he commanded the division that defended Little Kinmen, also called Lieyu, during the artillery battle of that year. The Ministry of National Defense says he was promoted to chief of the General Staff in December 1981, and Taiwan News says he held that post for eight years. He later served as minister of national defense and premier. He died on 30 March 2020, aged 101, according to both the ministry and Taiwan News.

In 2018, legislator Freddy Lim asked for an examination of the archived files so that the government could apologise to the victims' families. The Global Taiwan Institute reports that the defence minister of the time disagreed, saying the troops had followed the standard procedures of the martial law period. The ministry later said that, because so much time had passed, it would be too difficult to investigate the victims' names and backgrounds.

On 13 July 2022 the Control Yuan released an investigation report on what it called the "37 Incident." The Global Taiwan Institute describes the report as unprecedented in formally recognising the killings as unjustified. It concluded that the killings were the culmination of years of hostility toward refugees by the Kinmen garrison, and it found that similar acts had been committed in 1972. The report also found that the 1987 investigation left out evidence, did not identify the victims, and did not alert the Vietnamese authorities to their deaths. It asked the Ministry of National Defense to conduct its own inquiry into the original investigation, and to add refugee rights to military training. The Control Yuan member Kao Yong-cheng presented the findings, according to the Global Taiwan Institute and the Taipei Times. New Bloom Magazine says that the subsequent military court investigations were criticised as perfunctory, and that key details of how the refugees were shot were left out of the report.

The Taipei Times reports that commanding officers, including General Chao Wan-fu, lost their posts. Four officers were detained and first sentenced to more than two years in prison. On appeal the term fell to 20 to 22 months, with the sentence suspended, and they were allowed to remain in the army until retirement. New Bloom Magazine gives the same range and dates the sentences to December 1988, and says the Ministry of National Defense maintained that the soldiers had only been acting in accordance with their duties.

The Taipei Times notes that historian Kuan Jen-chien says the four dismissed officers later kept their military careers. Chao later rose to be deputy chief of the General Staff and an adviser on military strategy to the president. The Global Taiwan Institute says the military court argued that the defendants "took action out of duty and responsibility" and acted with "mercy."

The victims' relatives have pressed for answers. New Bloom Magazine names Tran Quoc Dung, who travelled to Taiwan to seek truth and reconciliation. The Taipei Times shows relatives at a 2024 press conference holding the names and photographs of the dead. The relatives, New Bloom Magazine says, have said that they did not come to blame Taiwan or its government, but hoped for the truth.

The Taipei Times says the families continue to seek answers. New Bloom Magazine argues that the Ministry of National Defense has continued to assert that the soldiers' actions were justified, even after the Control Yuan report. New Bloom Magazine notes that Taiwan still lacks an asylum law, and presents the case as part of a wider pattern of military and police wrongdoing covered up during the authoritarian period, and says it is still unclear whether there will be justice for the killings.
